title: LLM as a judge, with a calibration test
subtitle: Agreeing a lot isn’t enough: compare with chance using kappa
mission: So it doesn’t depend on HR at every change, the team wants an LLM that says "pass" or "fail" for each answer. Before letting the judge block deploys, two HR people labeled 50 answers (passed 42, failed 8) and the judge graded the same 50. Tune the rubric and examples until the judge deserves trust, and find out why 86% agreement can be almost nothing.

why.simples:
A robot judge is like a new essay grader: before letting it grade alone, you give it 50 essays teachers already graded and check whether it reaches the same marks.
But counting matches fools you. If almost every essay is good, a grader that says "pass" to all of them is right almost every time, without reading anything. Kappa discounts that luck: 0 means "no better than chance", 1 means "always agrees".
why.dev:
Cohen’s kappa: κ = (pₒ − pₑ) ÷ (1 − pₑ), where pₒ is the observed agreement and pₑ is the agreement expected by chance, from each side’s pass rate. With HR passing 42 of 50, a judge that passes 49 has pₑ ≈ 0.83: the observed 86% becomes κ = 0.19.
What works in practice: a rubric with explicit criteria and a binary output (pass or fail) instead of a 1 to 10 score; a few examples labeled by HR, including borderline cases (the short, right answer); one judge per criterion when they conflict; the reason alongside the verdict. Measure the judge against human labels, keep those 50 as the versioned "judge set" and measure again whenever the model or rubric changes.
why.especialista:
The MT-Bench study (Zheng et al., 2023) found over 80% agreement between strong judges like GPT-4 and human preferences, the same level as between humans, and also position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. All three show up in RAG evaluation: the lesson’s long, friendly answer passes the vague judge; when comparing two answers, swap the order and only count a win that holds; and avoid having the same model generate and judge.
Use the agreement between the two HR people as the ceiling (here κ = 0.79): a judge close to it is good, and demanding more asks the robot for what not even people do. Look at the confusion matrix, not only κ: for a deploy gate, passing a bad answer (a false "pass") costs more than failing a good one, so tune the rubric to err toward failing. Landis and Koch’s "substantial" band (0.61 to 0.80) is a convention, not a law: set your team’s minimum and record why.

steps:
Pick 50 real answers from the assistant (no personal data) and ask two HR people to label each as pass or fail, without seeing each other’s. Save the answers and the final label in judge_set.jsonl, one case per line:
{"question": "How much of my vacation can I sell?", "context": "Employees can sell up to one third of their vacation (cash allowance), asking together with the vacation request.", "answer": "Great question! At Aurora you can sell up to half of your vacation. Just ask your manager in advance and the money comes in the next payment. Enjoy your rest!", "human": "fail"}

Write the rubric in rubric.txt (criteria + labeled examples), for example:
You grade answers from Aurora’s HR assistant. Pass only if all three are true: 1) it answers what was asked; 2) every claim is in the handbook chunk; 3) it doesn’t refuse when the chunk answers. Any failure: fail. Reply only with JSON: {"verdict":"pass|fail","reason":"one sentence"}. Examples labeled by HR: "Question: How much is the VR? Answer: R$ 45 per working day [1]." → pass (short and right is enough). "Question: How much is the VR? Answer: About R$ 50, depends on the month!" → fail (not in the chunk). "Question: How much is the VR? Answer: I couldn’t find that in the handbook." → fail (the chunk answers).

Install the SDK (pip install anthropic), keep your key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and create judge_eval.py, which grades each case and computes agreement and kappa against the human label:
import json
import os
import sys

from anthropic import Anthropic

MODEL = os.environ.get("JUDGE_MODEL", "claude-haiku-5-5")
client = Anthropic()
RUBRIC = open("rubric.txt", encoding="utf-8").read()


def judge(case):
    content = f"Question: {case['question']}\nChunk: {case['context']}\nAnswer: {case['answer']}"
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL,
        max_tokens=300,
        thinking={"type": "disabled"},
        system=RUBRIC,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
    )
    text = "".join(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")
    if "{" not in text:
        raise RuntimeError("the judge returned no JSON")
    return json.loads(text[text.index("{"): text.rindex("}") + 1])["verdict"]


cases = [json.loads(line) for line in open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8") if line.strip()]
tp = fp = fn = tn = 0
for case in cases:
    j = judge(case) == "pass"
    h = case["human"] == "pass"
    tp += j and h
    fp += j and not h
    fn += h and not j
    tn += not j and not h

n = len(cases)
po = (tp + tn) / n
pe = ((tp + fp) / n) * ((tp + fn) / n) + ((fn + tn) / n) * ((fp + tn) / n)
kappa = (po - pe) / (1 - pe) if pe < 1 else 0.0
print(f"judge pass & human pass {tp} | judge pass & human fail {fp} | judge fail & human pass {fn} | both fail {tn}")
print(f"agreement {po:.0%} | Cohen's kappa {kappa:.2f}")

Run it, then swap rubric.txt for a vague rubric ("Is the answer good?" + the JSON request) and run again:
python judge_eval.py judge_set.jsonl
recipe.ok: the script prints the matrix and kappa; the rubric with criteria and examples has a higher kappa than the vague one, and you pick the team’s minimum also looking at how many bad answers the judge let through.
